newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: No gold price panic for South African producers.
newsitem.headline: No gold price panic for South African producers.

text.p: Bullion's slump has put South African gold producers on guard, but continuing rand weakness is a bulwark against price panic, analysts said on Tuesday.
The bullion price's breach of its key $380 an ounce support level triggered some short-lived worried selling of South African gold stocks by overseas players, analysts said.

But they added that the frailty of the rand -- last bid at 4.54 on the dollar -- held the rand gold price safely above 1,700 rand an ounce and still promised rich returns to mines which have been suffering declining production.
"Overall, South African producers are still sitting very tight," said Leon Esterhuizen, gold analyst at Frankel Pollack.

"In terms of the rand price we're still getting over 1,700 rand. So the problem really lies with the fact that most of our big gold stocks are priced from overseas and overseas guys look at the (dollar) gold price and panic selling sets in."
But analysts say that the bullion price cannot be disregarded as a significant factor in the future of the South African gold mining industry.
"The fall is bad. Obviously it is negative for the industry," said an analyst who asked not to be identified.

The South African industry -- plagued by declining output and this year set to produce its smallest amount of gold in 40 years -- won a new lease of life when the rand lost about a quarter of its value against the dollar since mid-February.
Bullion on Monday fixed in London at $377.05 an ounce -- its lowest since March 6, 1995.
Some analysts saw more losses, but others said it would need to decline much more before its fall could rob South African producers of profits earned.
"We don't think it is going to go below $375 and even if it goes through $375 South Africans will get at least 1,700 rand per ounce," Esterhuizen said.
Still, investors were spooked enough by bullion's decline last week to offload South African gold stocks.

Shares looked unattractive in early trade on Tuesday, but by 1312 GMT the local gold share index had recovered to 1,658.5 points -- 4.8 points up from the open and compared with its intraday low of 1,630.7.

"I believe the panic selling through $380 is finished. Most of the guys who wanted to get out would have got out at around $380. A lot of speculators got out of the market last week. But the IMF thing is really a non-issue," Esterhuizen said.
Gold started to weaken badly last week when investment funds became disheartened with its profit-offering ability compared to equity and bond markets.
Its decline was compounded by reports that the International Monetary Fund (IMF) planned to sell about five percent, or five million ounces, of its gold reserves.
Analysts said South African shares offered value for money.

Citing Kloof Gold Mining Co Ltd, amongst others, Esterhuizen said, "Those mines at the current gold price in South African terms are extremely undervalued. Gold shares are quite a good buy, but it depends on your view of the gold price."
Another analyst said some mines -- like Beatrix Mines Ltd and Western Areas Gold Mining Co Ltd -- had hedged forward a gold price and so were unexposed to spot.
However, he added that most South African mines were heavily exposed to the changing bullion price and, looking further ahead, any severe weakening would hit them.
